steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a systems paper presenting PICO, a pipeline framework for cooperative CNN inference across several heterogeneous mobile devices. Explain why cooperative inference is attractive, what challenges earlier work left open, how PICO works at a high level, our results, contributions, and the paper organization.

steps.text:

- Why devices can't do it alone (and can't just upload)
- Cooperative inference across devices
- Open challenges
- PICO: the pipeline idea and optimization goal
- Approach, experiments, contributions, organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Mobile devices, data, and CNN inference
  - explosive growth of mobile devices; large volume of data (images, videos)
  - versatile CNNs with pre-trained parameters for decisions on raw data (CNN inference)
  - applications: smart home, intelligent factory, automatic driving (cite)
- Obstacles
  - resource-limited devices; compute not enough vs datacenter
  - wireless network not ready for massive raw data; autopilot camera >700 MB video per second (cite); upload -> significant latency
  - privacy concern in uploading to cloud (cite)
- Cooperative inference
  - spatial independence of convolution -> split conv layer input/output into tiles on different devices
  - recent attention (cite)
  - procedure: data source splits raw data into tiles, distributes over wireless, devices execute one or several layers, source gathers + stitches; iterate until all layers done
  - privacy (data stays local), lower latency near source
  - vs model compression / parameter pruning (cite): no accuracy loss, no re-training
- Open challenges
  - (1) redundant calculation: output scalar = dot product of kernel and input subregion; kernel bigger than 1\times 1 -> overlapping input tiles; overlap grows recursively over multiple layers; communication expensive -> choose layers carefully
  - (2) DAG structures: ResNet34 (cite) skip-connections, InceptionV3 (cite) multiple branches; huge number of choices; prior work mainly chains (cite)
  - (3) diverse/heterogeneous device resources
- PICO
  - explore prior parallelization work; pipeline cooperation framework; Fig. 1
  - CNN graph + devices divided into 3 stages forming pipeline; each stage: small CNN segment + subset of devices -> less communication and redundant calculation
  - metrics: latency (sum over stages), period (longest stage latency); lower period tends to raise latency
  - goal: minimize redundant calculation and period (max throughput), latency under a certain value
- Approach, experiments, contributions, organization
  - formulate pipeline inference; NP-Hard to get optimum directly
  - two-step: orchestrate graph into chain of pieces with minimum redundant calculation; choose best partition of pieces and devices; dynamic programming
  - 2\sim 8 Raspberry-Pi devices; throughput up 1.8\sim 6.8\times under different CPU frequencies / device counts
  - contributions: PICO framework; graph splitting algorithm; optimal stage settings algorithm; Raspberry-Pi cluster evaluation on image recognition and object detection
  - Sections II–VIII

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been an explosive growth of mobile devices. Because there are so many mobile devices, they provide a large volume of data (images, videos, etc.). At the same time, versatile convolution neural networks (CNN) with pre-trained parameters have become powerful tools for making intelligent decisions from this raw data (CNN inference). Embedding CNN into mobile devices makes many intelligent applications possible, such as smart home, intelligent factory, and even automatic driving.

One obstacle to this embedding is that mobile devices have limited resources. The computing capability of mobile devices, compared with a datacenter, is not enough to do CNN inference on their own. On the other hand, the current wireless network is not ready to transmit the massive volume of raw data that these mobile devices collect. For example, an autopilot camera could capture more than 700 MB of video every second, and uploading all of this video data to the datacenter would cause significant network latency. Also, uploading data from user devices to the cloud always raises concerns about privacy.

Because the convolution operation is spatially independent, the input and output (feature) of convolutional (conv) layers can be split into several small tiles and executed on different devices. So cooperative CNN inference on multiple mobile devices has recently got the attention of researchers. In the inference procedure, the data source (camera, sensors, etc.) captures raw data and splits it into tiles. The tiles are distributed through a wireless network to multiple nearby mobile devices, which execute them independently using one or several layers. Then the data source gathers all the output tiles and stitches them together to get the result. This procedure is repeated multiple times until all the layers are executed. Cooperative inference also protects user privacy, because all the data stays local. Also, being closer to the data source means lower network latency. Compared with other strategies like model compression and parameter pruning, cooperative inference does not lose inference accuracy and does not need the model to be re-trained.

- Open challenges
  - (1) redundant calculation: output scalar = dot product of kernel and input subregion; kernel bigger than 1\times 1 -> overlapping input tiles; overlap grows recursively over layers; communication expensive -> choose layers carefully
  - (2) DAG structures: ResNet34 (cite) skip-connections, InceptionV3 (cite) branches; huge number of choices; prior work mainly chains (cite)
  - (3) heterogeneous device resources
- PICO
  - pipeline cooperation framework; Fig. 1; 3 stages, each a CNN segment + subset of devices
  - latency (sum over stages) vs period (longest stage); goal: min redundant calculation + period, latency bounded
- Approach and results
  - NP-Hard; two-step DP: pieces in a chain, then partition pieces + devices
  - 2\sim 8 Raspberry-Pi devices; 1.8\sim 6.8\times throughput
- Contributions (4 bullets) and paper organization (Sections II–VIII)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been an explosive growth of mobile devices. Because there are so many mobile devices, they provide a large volume of data (images, videos, etc.). At the same time, versatile convolution neural networks (CNN) with pre-trained parameters have become powerful tools for making intelligent decisions from this raw data (CNN inference). Embedding CNN into mobile devices makes many intelligent applications possible, such as smart home, intelligent factory, and even automatic driving.

One obstacle to this embedding is that mobile devices have limited resources. The computing capability of mobile devices, compared with a datacenter, is not enough to do CNN inference on their own. On the other hand, the current wireless network is not ready to transmit the massive volume of raw data that these mobile devices collect. For example, an autopilot camera could capture more than 700 MB of video every second, and uploading all of this video data to the datacenter would cause significant network latency. Also, uploading data from user devices to the cloud always raises concerns about privacy.

Because the convolution operation is spatially independent, the input and output (feature) of convolutional (conv) layers can be split into several small tiles and executed on different devices. So cooperative CNN inference on multiple mobile devices has recently got the attention of researchers. In the inference procedure, the data source (camera, sensors, etc.) captures raw data and splits it into tiles. The tiles are distributed through a wireless network to multiple nearby mobile devices, which execute them independently using one or several layers. Then the data source gathers all the output tiles and stitches them together to get the result. This procedure is repeated multiple times until all the layers are executed. Cooperative inference also protects user privacy, because all the data stays local. Also, being closer to the data source means lower network latency. Compared with other strategies like model compression and parameter pruning, cooperative inference does not lose inference accuracy and does not need the model to be re-trained.

But even with all these benefits, some challenges are still not completely solved in previous works. The input feature can be executed in parallel, but (1) the parallelism introduces redundant calculation because of the property of CNN. Each scalar in the output feature of a conv layer is calculated by a dot product of the conv kernel and a subregion of the input feature. In most cases the kernel size is bigger than 1\times 1, so the input tiles of the partitioned input feature have to overlap with each other so that the scalars at the edge of the output tiles are correct. And the overlapped part grows recursively when devices execute multiple layers in one iteration of the inference procedure, while communication is expensive for mobile devices. So the executed layers have to be chosen carefully. Also, (2) the structures of many CNNs are directed acyclic graphs (DAG) and not chains. ResNet34 uses skip-connection technology, which lets a layer connect directly to another deeper layer. InceptionV3 has a structure with multiple branches to capture more information from the input feature. Because of these complex structures there is a huge number of possible choices. Previous works mainly focused on the chain structure, which is much easier than DAG. And (3) compared with a datacenter, the computing resources of mobile devices are diverse, and this heterogeneous environment also makes optimizing cooperative inference harder.

In this paper we explore previous works on parallelizing CNN inference and propose a pipeline cooperation (PICO) framework to accelerate inference on diverse mobile devices. Fig. 1 shows a diagrammatic sketch of the framework. PICO divides the whole CNN graph and the mobile devices into 3 stages, and these stages make up an efficient inference pipeline. Each stage has a small segment of the original CNN and a subset of the mobile devices, so both the communication overhead and the redundant calculation can be reduced significantly. A pipeline has two important metrics, latency and period. Latency is the sum of the inference latencies of all the stages, and period is the longest latency among the stages. Obviously, decreasing the period tends to increase the latency. Our optimization goal is to minimize the redundant calculation and the period (maximize throughput) while keeping the latency of the pipeline under a certain value.

First we formulate the pipeline inference, and then we analyze the complexity of the optimization problem and find that obtaining the optimal result directly is NP-Hard. Based on this analysis, PICO uses a two-step optimization to maximize throughput. In the first step we orchestrate the CNN graph into a sequence of pieces, which have the minimum redundant calculation inside and make up the original CNN graph in a chain structure. Then we choose the best partition of these pieces and devices to build the inference pipeline. The algorithms in these procedures are based on dynamic programming.

In our experiment we evaluate the PICO framework with 2\sim 8 Raspberry-Pi devices. The throughput is improved by 1.8\sim 6.8\times under different CPU frequencies and numbers of devices.

In short, our contributions are the following:

- • We present a pipeline cooperation (PICO) framework that accelerates CNN inference with diverse mobile devices.

- • We propose an algorithm that splits the complex CNN graph structure into more fine-grained pieces.

- • We propose an algorithm that decides the optimal stage settings of the inference pipeline to maximize the throughput.

- • We apply our technique to a cluster of Raspberry-Pi-based hardware and evaluate image recognition and object detection CNN models.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section II gives background on CNN and different parallelization strategies in mobile devices. Section III formulates the inference process and gives a cost model for the optimization. Sections IV and V describe our approach for finding near-optimal parallelization. Section VI presents the evaluation results. Section VII details the related work and Section VIII concludes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent years have witnessed an explosive growth of mobile devices. The huge number of mobile devices provides a large volume of data (images, videos, etc.). Meanwhile, versatile convolution neural networks (CNN) with pre-trained parameters have become powerful tools for making intelligent decisions from these raw data (CNN inference). Embedding CNN in mobile devices enables many intelligent applications to become reality, such as smart home, intelligent factory, and even automatic driving [1,2].

One obstacle to the embedding is the resource-limited mobile devices. Compared with a datacenter, the computing capability of mobile devices is not enough to perform CNN inference alone. On the other hand, the current wireless network is not prepared for transmitting the massive volume of raw data collected by these mobile devices. For example, an autopilot camera could capture more than 700 MB of video every second [3], and uploading all the video data to the datacenter would bring significant network latency. Moreover, uploading data from user devices to the cloud always raises privacy concerns [3].

Benefiting from the spatial independence of the convolution operation, the input and output (feature) of convolutional (conv) layers can be split into several small tiles and executed on different devices. As a consequence, cooperative CNN inference on multiple mobile devices has recently gained the attention of researchers [4,5,6]. During the inference procedure, the data source (camera, sensors, etc.) captures raw data and splits it into tiles. These tiles are distributed to multiple nearby mobile devices through a wireless network and executed independently using one or several layers. The data source is then responsible for gathering all the output tiles and stitching them to obtain the result. The procedure is iterated multiple times until all layers are executed. Cooperative inference also protects user privacy since all the data stay local. Moreover, the closer to the data source, the lower the network latency. Compared with other strategies such as model compression and parameter pruning [7,8,9], cooperative inference neither loses inference accuracy nor requires re-training the model.

However, despite all these benefits, some challenges remain that are not completely solved in previous works. Although the input feature can be executed in parallel, (1) the parallelism introduces redundant calculation due to the property of CNN. The scalar in the output feature of one conv layer is calculated through a dot product of the conv kernel and a subregion of the input feature. In most cases the kernel size is bigger than 1\times 1, so the input tiles of the partitioned input feature overlap with each other to guarantee that the scalars at the edge of the output tiles are correct. Moreover, the overlapped part increases recursively when devices execute multiple layers during one iteration of the inference procedure, but communication is expensive for mobile devices. As a consequence, the executed layers need to be carefully chosen. However, (2) the structures of many CNNs are directed acyclic graphs (DAG) rather than chains. ResNet34 [10] uses skip-connection technology that allows a layer to connect directly to another deeper layer. The structure of InceptionV3 [11] contains multiple branches to capture more information from the input feature. These complex structures lead to a huge number of possible choices. Previous works mainly focused on the chain structure [4,5,6], which is much easier than DAG. Compared with a datacenter, (3) the computing resources of mobile devices are diverse, and the heterogeneous environment also hinders the optimization of cooperative inference.

In this paper, we explore previous works on parallelizing CNN inference and propose a pipeline cooperation (PICO) framework for accelerating inference on diverse mobile devices. Fig. 1 plots a diagrammatic sketch of our framework. PICO divides the entire CNN graph and the mobile devices into 3 stages, which compose an efficient inference pipeline. Since each stage owns a small segment of the original CNN and a subset of mobile devices, both the communication overhead and the redundant calculation can be significantly reduced. There are two important metrics for a pipeline: latency and period. The first is the sum of the inference latencies of all stages and the second is the longest latency among stages. Obviously, decreasing the period tends to increase the latency. Our optimization goal is to minimize the redundant calculation and period (maximize throughput) while keeping the latency of the pipeline under a certain value.

We first formulate the pipeline inference, then analyze the complexity of the optimization problem and find that it is NP-Hard to obtain the optimal result directly. Based on our analysis, PICO uses a two-step optimization to maximize the throughput. In the first step, we orchestrate the CNN graph into a sequence of pieces. These pieces have the minimum redundant calculation inside and compose the original CNN graph in a chain structure. Then we choose the best partition of these pieces and devices to construct the inference pipeline. The algorithms used in these procedures are based on dynamic programming.

In our experiment we use 2\sim 8 Raspberry-Pi devices to evaluate the PICO framework. The throughput can be improved by 1.8\sim 6.8\times under different CPU frequencies and numbers of devices.

In a nutshell, we make the following contributions:

- • We present a pipeline cooperation (PICO) framework to accelerate CNN inference with diverse mobile devices.

- • We propose an algorithm to split the complex CNN graph structure into more fine-grained pieces.

- • We propose an algorithm to decide the optimal stage settings for the inference pipeline that maximize the throughput.

- • We apply our technique on a cluster of Raspberry-Pi-based hardware and evaluate image recognition and object detection CNN models.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II provides background on CNN and different parallelization strategies in mobile devices. Section III formulates the inference process and gives a cost model for further optimization. Sections IV and V describe our approach to finding near-optimal parallelization. Section VI presents the results of our evaluation. Section VII details the related work and Section VIII concludes.

References:
[1] G. Kour and R. Saabne, “Real-time segmentation of on-line handwritten arabic script,” in Frontiers in Handwriting Recognition (ICFHR) . IEEE, 2014.
[2] ——, “Fast classification of handwritten on-line arabic characters,” in Soft Computing and Pattern Recognition (SoCPaR) . IEEE, 2014.
[3] Z. Zhou, X. Chen, E. Li, L. Zeng, K. Luo, and J. Zhang, “Edge intelligence: Paving the last mile of artificial intelligence with edge computing,” Proceedings of the IEEE , 2019.

[6] L. Zhou, M. H. Samavatian, A. Bacha, S. Majumdar, and R. Teodorescu, “Adaptive parallel execution of deep neural networks on heterogeneous edge devices,” in Proceedings of the 4th ACM/IEEE Symposium on Edge Computing , 2019.

[10] K. He, X. Zhang, S. Ren, and J. Sun, “Deep residual learning for image recognition,” in IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition (CVPR) , 2016.
